newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Main hurdle to Brazzaville truce cleared-UN envoy.
newsitem.headline: Main hurdle to Brazzaville truce cleared-UN envoy.

text.p: U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said on Friday he had cleared the main obstacle to a truce accord in fighting in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville by resolving a dispute over who should sign it.
"We obtained the agreement of both parties to sign the ceasefire document," Sanoun told Reuters from neighbouring Gabon, a day after visiting Brazzaville.
"They were going to sign over the evening (of Thursday) and present us with the document today," he added.
President Pascal Lissouba last week refused to sign a ceasefire with his rival in the conflict, former military ruler Denis Sassou Nguesso.
Lisouba said his prime minister should sign as Sassou was not a head of state. Sassou insisted it had to be Lisouba or no deal. Mediators failed to reconcile the two.
"Yesterday the president agreed to sign the document himself, so we've resolved that problem," said Sahnoun.

"The next step is to try and bring the parties to Libreville to substantive negotiations on the political issues on how to create an environment conducive to elections, on national reconciliation," he added.
The veteran Algerian diplomat is mediating for the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity in turbulent Central Africa.
There was no immediate comment from Lissouba's camp but Sassou's spokesman Francois Iboovi said only that his boss was studying the latest ceasefire proposals.
Gabon's President Omar Bongo, a son-in-law of Sassou and friend of Lissouba, is trying to rally the rivals around a July 14 ceasefire, Iboovi told Reuters.
He said by telephone that Sassou was assessing the new initiative for a truce between his militia and forces supporting Lissouba and would reply shortly.
"We have received the proposals from Omar Bongo and we are studying them. The date for the ceasefire is part of the proposals. It won't be long before we respond," Iboovi said.
Clashes which began on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militias, have killed hundreds of people, mainly civilians.
Sahnoun said Brazzaville, which is across the Congo river from the Democratic Congo capital, Kinshasa, was calm on Thursday and he was able to tour several districts.
Aid workers reported brief outbursts of firing late on Thursday and at daybreak on Friday, a pattern in recent days.
Iboovi said the Bongo proposals almost exclusively dealt with conditions for a ceasefire.

Brazzaville mayor, Bernard Kolelas, is heading a national mediation effort. His militia were at the heart of similar political and ethnic clashes which killed at least 2,000 people after a disputed 1993 election.
Lissouba had been planning to run for re-election on July 27. Sassou and Kolelas were also planning to stand.
